summary: Applies the IPv6 over NBMA architecture to ATM networks. It allows normal host behavior for neighbor discovery while also permitting shortcut ATM connections. It is a proposed standard and was updated by RFC 8064.

plainLanguage.summary: ATM carries traffic over virtual circuits: permanent ones set up by an administrator, and switched ones set up per call. RFC 2492 says how IPv6 packets are carried over such a link. It fills in the ATM-specific parts: how a packet is wrapped, how big it may be, and how each interface names itself.

questions: how is ipv6 carried over atm
what is the default mtu for ipv6 over atm
what is null encapsulation in ipv6 over atm
how are ipv6 interface tokens built on atm
subtitle: The ATM-specific details for carrying IPv6 packets over permanent and switched ATM circuits.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs concrete rules for each kind of link. ATM links are connection-oriented and have no broadcast, so the general IPv6 over NBMA architecture needs ATM-specific code points.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes the AAL5 and LLC/SNAP encapsulation, the default MTU of 9180 bytes, the encoding of the Neighbor Discovery link-layer address option, and several ways to build interface tokens, for both PVC and SVC modes.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 8064. A minimal IPv6/ATM driver only has to support PVC mode.

today: RFC 2492 is a Proposed Standard published in January 1999 and is updated by RFC 8064. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document is an ATM-specific companion to the ION working group's architecture document, IPv6 over Non Broadcast Multiple Access networks. Terminology and architectural descriptions are not repeated there. The use of ATM to provide point to point PVC service, or flexible point to point and point to multipoint SVC service, is covered by this document.

A minimally conforming IPv6/ATM driver SHALL support the PVC mode of operation. An IPv6/ATM driver that supports the full SVC mode SHALL also support PVC mode of operation.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the ATM companion to the general rules for running IPv6 on a link that has no broadcast. ATM traffic travels over virtual circuits: a permanent one that an administrator sets up, or a switched one that is set up per call. A driver that does the minimum has to support the permanent kind only.

sections.title: Permanent Virtual Circuit Environments
sections.content:
When the ATM network is used in PVC mode, each PVC connects exactly two nodes, and the use of Neighbor Discovery and other IPv6 features is limited. IPv6/ATM interfaces have only one neighbour on each link. The MARS and NHRP protocols are not necessary, since multicast and broadcast operations collapse down to an ATM level unicast operation. Dynamically discovered shortcuts are not supported.

Since ATM PVC links do not use link-layer addresses, the link-layer address options SHOULD not be included in any Neighbor Discovery message. If a link-layer address option is present in a Neighbor Discovery message, then the option SHOULD be ignored.

The document notes that this use of PVC links neither mandates nor prohibits the use of extensions to the Neighbor Discovery protocol that may be developed for general use or for use in PVC connections, for example Inverse Neighbor Discovery. A minimally conforming IPv6/ATM driver SHALL support the PVC mode of operation, and PVC only implementations are not required to support any SVC mode of operation.
sections.plainLanguage: On a permanent circuit the link has exactly one neighbour at the other end, so the tricks that a shared link needs do not apply. There is no multicast to organise and no shortcut to discover, and the address options in a Neighbor Discovery message are ignored.

sections.title: Encapsulation and MTU on a PVC
sections.content:
Following the model in the multiprotocol encapsulation document, AAL5 SHALL be the default Adaptation Layer service, and LLC/SNAP encapsulation SHALL be the default encapsulation used by unicast and multicast packets across point to point PVC links. The default IPv6 packet encapsulation is:

[0xAA-AA-03][0x00-00-00][0x86-DD][IPv6 packet]
    (LLC)       (OUI)     (PID)

IPv6/ATM drivers MAY also support null encapsulation as a configurable option. When null encapsulation is enabled, the IPv6 packet is passed directly to the AAL5 layer. Both ends of the PVC MUST be configured to use null encapsulation, and the PVC will not be available for use by protocols other than IPv6. The concatenation of IPv6 over PPP with PPP over AAL5 PVCs is not covered by this specification.

The default IP MTU size for PVC links is 9180 bytes. Other IP MTU values MAY be used.
sections.plainLanguage: On a permanent circuit an IPv6 packet is wrapped in eight octets: three of LLC, three of organisation code, and two carrying the value 0x86-DD that says IPv6. A driver may also be set up to send the packet with no wrapper at all, but then the circuit can carry IPv6 only. The largest packet is 9180 bytes.

sections.title: Encapsulation on a Switched Virtual Circuit
sections.content:
On SVC links the default Adaptation Layer service is again AAL5, and the default encapsulation is again LLC/SNAP. The default IPv6 unicast packet encapsulation is the same as on a PVC. The default IPv6 multicast packet encapsulation is:

[0xAA-AA-03][0x00-00-5E][0x00-01][pkt$cmi][0x86DD][IPv6 packet]
    (LLC)       (OUI)     (PID)    (mars encaps)

The driver's Cluster Member ID SHALL be copied into the 2 octet pkt$cmi field prior to transmission.

Null encapsulation MAY also be used on an SVC, but only for passing IPv6 packets from one IPv6/ATM driver to another, and SHALL NOT be used on the point to point SVC between the driver and its local MARS. Both ends of the SVC MUST agree to use null encapsulation during the call SETUP phase, and the SVC will not be available for use by protocols other than IPv6. If null encapsulation is enabled on data SVCs between routers, inter-router NHRP traffic SHALL utilize a separate, parallel SVC. Use of null encapsulation is not encouraged when IPv6/ATM is used with MARS, NHRP and Neighbor Discovery.

The encapsulation of MARS control messages remains the same as shown in the multicast support document, and NHRP control messages remain as shown in the NHRP document. Both use the same wrapper shape, with the PID 0x00-03. For MARS control messages the mar$afn field remains 0x0F for ATM addresses, the mar$pro field SHALL be 0x86DD for IPv6, and the mar$op.version field remains 0x00 for MARS. For NHRP control messages the ar$afn field remains 0x0F, the ar$pro field SHALL be 0x86DD, and the ar$op.version field remains 0x01 for NHRP.

Section 5.2 of the NBMA architecture document describes the Neighbor Discovery link-layer address option. For IPv6/ATM drivers the subfields SHALL be encoded in a particular manner. The NTL field defines the type and length of the ATM number that immediately follows the STL field. Its most significant bit is reserved and MUST be set to zero. The second most significant bit is a flag: x = 0 means the ATM number is in ATM Forum AESA format, and x = 1 means native E.164 format. The bottom 6 bits give the length of the associated ATM address field in octets. The STL field has the same format and defines the length of the subaddress field if it exists; if it does not exist the entire octet field MUST be zero, and if it does exist it will be in AESA format, so the flag SHALL be zero. The NBMA Number field is a variable length field containing the ATM address of the link layer target and is always present. The NBMA Subaddress field may or may not be present, and when it is not the option ends after the NBMA Number. The octet ordering of the two fields SHALL be the same as that used in MARS and NHRP control messages.
sections.plainLanguage: On a switched circuit the same wrapper is used, and multicast packets get two extra fields so the receiver can tell which group the packet belongs to. Control messages for the multicast and next-hop protocols get their own wrapper. The Neighbor Discovery option that carries a link-layer address has a defined layout, with one bit for the address format and six bits for its length.

sections.title: UNI 3.0/3.1 Signalling and MTU
sections.content:
When an IPv6 node places a call to another IPv6 node, it SHOULD follow the procedures in the ATM signalling support and default IP MTU documents for signalling UNI 3.0/3.1 SVCs and negotiating MTU. The default IP MTU size on a logical link is 9180 bytes.

The document notes that while the procedures in the default MTU document still apply to IPv6 over ATM, IPv6 Path MTU Discovery is used by nodes and routers rather than IPv4 MTU discovery. IPv6 nodes are not required to implement Path MTU Discovery, but IPv6/ATM nodes SHOULD implement it. Since IPv6 nodes negotiate an appropriate MTU for each virtual circuit, Path MTU should never be triggered, since neither node should ever receive a Packet Too Big message to trigger Path MTU Discovery. When nodes are communicating via one or more routers, Path MTU Discovery will be used just as it is for legacy networks.
sections.plainLanguage: When a node dials another node, the two sides agree a maximum packet size during the call setup, 9180 bytes by default. IPv6 finds oversized packets on the path with Path MTU Discovery rather than the older IPv4 method.

sections.title: Interface Tokens
sections.content:
For both PVC and SVC modes of operation, one of the following methods SHALL be used to generate interface tokens as required by the IPv6 addressing architecture.

Based on ESI values, when the underlying ATM interface is identified by an ATM End System Address, the interface token MAY be formed as a one octet field always set to 0, a six octet ESI field, and a one octet SEL field. The bit corresponding to the EUI-64 Global/Local bit is always reset, indicating that this address is not a globally unique IPv6 interface token.

Based on 48 bit MAC values, where the underlying ATM NIC driver has access to one or more 48 bit MAC values unique to the NIC, the IPv6/ATM interface MAY use one of these values to create a unique interface token. Based on EUI-64 values, where the driver has access to one or more 64 bit EUI-64 values unique to the NIC, the interface SHOULD use one of these values to create a unique interface token, after inverting the Global/Local identifier bit. When EUI-64 values are used, the only modification allowed to the octet string read from the NIC is inversion of the Global/Local identifier bit.

Based on Native E.164 addresses, when an interface uses Native E.164 addresses the E.164 values MAY be used to generate an interface token from the digits in semi-octets, that is, two digits per octet. The EUI-64 Global/Local indicator is set to 0, indicating that this is not a globally unique IPv6 interface token.

If no MAC, EUI-64, AESA or E.164 value is available for generating an interface token, then the interface token SHALL be generated as described in the appendix of the IPv6 addressing architecture document. Where a logical ATM interface is associated with a different SEL field of a common AESA prefix, or a set of entirely separate ESIs has been registered with the local ATM switch to create a range of unique AESAs, the minimum information required to uniquely identify each logical ATM interface is their ESI+SEL combination. For the vhost case, vhost SHALL select a different interface token from the range of 64 bit values available to the ATM NIC, and each vhost SHALL implement its interfaces in such a way that no two or more vhosts end up advertising the same interface token onto the same logical link.
sections.plainLanguage: Each IPv6 interface needs an identifier that is unique on its link. The document gives four ways to build one: from the ESI and SEL of the ATM address, from a 48-bit MAC value, from a 64-bit EUI-64 value, or from an E.164 number. If the hardware has none of those, another documented method applies. Two virtual hosts on one card must not pick the same identifier.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: While this proposal does not introduce any new security mechanisms, all current IPv6 security mechanisms will work without modification for ATM. This includes both authentication and encryption for both Neighbor Discovery protocols as well as the exchange of IPv6 data packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is needed for security on ATM. The IPv6 mechanisms for authentication and encryption work as they do on any other link.
